bursts.order_text: Give Roman Navy the Rostrum and dolphin

Secure Messana using the forces and ships Rome already has. Arrange for the Roman Navy to collect Legio I from its present location and carry it to Messana, using successive crossings if necessary. Keep the Rhegian Punitive Legion supplied and paid. Delegate the commanders, embarkation arrangements, provisioning and routine administration to suitable people.
Seek any necessary Senate authorization and allocate up to 3,000 from the Roman treasury for this operation, keeping my personal money separate. Do not raise another fleet or duplicate an existing transport project. If a practical obstacle arises, arrange a reasonable alternative within these limits; bring me only decisions requiring additional authority or money.
Separately, appoint someone independent of me to examine the accusation that I diverted public funds. Give them access to the relevant public and household accounts, and require a finding based on evidence.
Privately send an agent to learn Syracuse’s military strength and intentions. Call this mission “Blue Olive”; keep its existence, agent and reports confidential. Send findings to me privately and distinguish observation from rumour.
Publicly seek a ceasefire with Hieron while maintaining our protection of Messana and its self-rule. Refusal or silence does not authorize further escalation.
Report the progress of transport, funding, the accounts inquiry, intelligence and diplomacy separately. Record what was ordered, what actually happened, and what remains unresolved. Quote only words someone actually said or wrote.

chats.body: I will say it to your face, since you will hear it anyway: Fictional senatorial associate
I fear a war with Carthage is coming. Messena and Sicily is not safe, i need your support to raise more armies and a navy to prepare

You shall have my support in asking the Senate for a defensive levy and ships fit to guard the straits. But let us not proclaim Carthage our enemy before she gives us cause; a fleet raised openly for Sicily may turn fear into war. I will stand with you when we put the measure before the Senate.
Do you believe I have taken funds from Rome? I am no traitor

No, Clepsina; I have no grounds to believe you have taken Rome’s funds, and I will not call you a traitor without proof. Let the accounts be examined plainly—an honest man should not have to hide from the reckoning.
Good. When the accounts are opened, I shall judge what is written there—not what men whisper.
Why do you accuse me so plainly of theft? do you have something against me or are you plotting to take my position?

I called it theft because I suspect goods were taken under your authority—but suspicion is not proof, and I have no witness to your own hand. I have no design on your consulship, Clepsina; it is shared with Blasio for this year, not mine to snatch. If you ask what grounds my suspicion, I’ll name them plainly—or withdraw the charge if I have none.
I cannot name them, Clepsina. I have only suspicion that goods were taken under your authority; no witness to your hand, and no proof. I spoke too strongly. I withdraw the charge against you.
Keep your thanks, Clepsina; I owed you the truth once I had no proof. Let us leave the matter there.
I have a favour to ask of you, as a friend: Find material that could weaken Clepsina without exposing the inquiry..

chronicle.title: Spurius Carvilius Maximus and Tiberius Coruncanius Support a Roman Fleet
chronicle.body: In the Senate debate, Spurius Carvilius Maximus supported authorizing a Roman fleet to defend Rome’s interests and protect her allies. Tiberius Coruncanius also supported the fleet, arguing that it should protect the Greek cities of the south.

quote.line: Rome must guard the allies who trust her.
quote.speaker: Spurius Carvilius Maximus
quote.occasion: in the Senate debate on a Roman fleet

chronicle.title: Quintus Ogulnius Gallus Opens Debate on Roman Silver for the Allies
chronicle.body: Quintus Ogulnius Gallus opened a Senate deliberation on using Roman silver to support Rome’s allies.

chronicle.title: Tiberius Coruncanius and Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges Debate a Roman Fleet
chronicle.body: In the Senate, the senator Tiberius Coruncanius argued that the southern Greeks must see Roman ships. The senator Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges argued that a fleet could guard Rome’s allies without another costly campaign.

quote.line: A fleet can guard allies without another costly campaign.
quote.speaker: Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges
quote.occasion: Senate debate on authorizing a fleet

chronicle.title: Roman Senators Support Aid to Rome’s Allies
chronicle.body: Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges publicly supported the Senate proposal to use Roman silver to support Rome’s allies. In the Senate, Spurius Carvilius Maximus argued that allied arms needed Roman silver, while Lucius Papirius Cursor spoke in favor of paying the allies who stood with Rome.

quote.line: Pay the allies who stand with us.
quote.speaker: Lucius Papirius Cursor
quote.occasion: in the Senate, speaking for aid to Rome’s allies

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina Offers Syracuse a Ceasefire
chronicle.body: The Roman consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina wrote to Hieron II, king of Syracuse, proposing a ceasefire at Messana. Rome would continue to protect the city from attack while respecting its self-rule and local laws, and both sides would refrain from hostilities during talks. Clepsina also ordered that the existing naval transport order be used to carry Legio I to Messana in successive crossings if needed. Meanwhile, Aristodemus’s family began arranging a marriage, and he intended to seek a suitable match through private negotiation.

changes.label: Aristodemus
changes.detail: enters the record under League of the Islanders

chronicle.title: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio Breaks His Promise to Gaius Genucius Clepsina
chronicle.body: The Roman consul Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio had promised the Roman consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina that he would stand with him when they put the measure before the Senate, but he broke that promise. Gaius Fabricius Luscinus had promised Clepsina that he would not call him a traitor without proof.

changes.label: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio
changes.detail: broke a promise to Gaius Genucius Clepsina: i will stand with you when we put the measure before the Senate.

quote.line: I will not call you a traitor without proof.
quote.speaker: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus
quote.occasion: to Gaius Genucius Clepsina, in making his promise

chronicle.title: Senators Back Using Roman Silver to Support Rome’s Allies
chronicle.body: In the Senate, the senator Gaius Claudius Canina publicly backed a proposal to use Roman silver to support Rome’s allies. The senator Publius Valerius Laevinus argued that allied arms needed Roman silver. The senator Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges urged spending silver where it would keep allies in the field, while the senator Lucius Postumius Megellus argued that paying the allies would win Rome glory.

quote.line: Pay the allies; let them win Rome's glory.
quote.speaker: Lucius Postumius Megellus
quote.occasion: Publicly backing the Senate proposal

chronicle.title: Senate Authorizes and Funds the Anio Water Works
chronicle.body: The Senate approved public authorization and funding for the Anio water works by 76 votes to none, with 24 abstentions. The patrician houses and landed families supported the measure, as did the Fabrician, Curian, Fabian, Coruncanian, and Claudian circles; the plebeian new men abstained. Lucius Papirius Cursor, Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, Spurius Carvilius Maximus, and Tiberius Coruncanius spoke for it, while Lucius Postumius Megellus spoke against it. The vote granted leave and funding, and the works awaited a further order to begin.

chronicle.title: Three Romans Support a Fleet to Defend Rome’s Interests
chronicle.body: Spurius Carvilius Maximus, Tiberius Coruncanius, and Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges each spoke in support of a Roman fleet to defend Rome’s interests.

chronicle.title: Laevinus, Gurges, Megellus, and Blasio Back Silver for Rome’s Allies
chronicle.body: Publius Valerius Laevinus publicly supported using Roman silver to aid Rome’s allies, arguing that their arms needed Roman money. Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges and Lucius Postumius Megellus also publicly backed the Senate proposal: Gurges urged spending where it would keep the allies in the field, while Megellus favored paying them so they could win glory for Rome. In the Senate, the consul Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio spoke for the proposal, arguing that Roman silver must keep the allies useful in the field.

quote.line: Roman silver must keep our allies useful in the field.
quote.speaker: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio
quote.occasion: in the Senate, speaking for the proposal

chronicle.title: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus Urges Treasury Funding for the Messana Operation
chronicle.body: In the Senate, Gaius Fabricius Luscinus spoke in support of authorizing up to 3,000 from the treasury for the Messana operation. He argued that the strait had to be held and the treasury should answer for it.

quote.line: The strait must be held, and the treasury must answer for it.
quote.speaker: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus
quote.occasion: to the Senate, in support of funding the Messana operation

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina Names Manius Curius Dentatus Admiral
chronicle.body: A faction formed around Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, and another around Manius Curius Dentatus. The Roman consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina named Curius admiral of the Roman fleet. A faction formed around Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges, and another around Tiberius Coruncanius.

chronicle.title: Roman Navy takes up the Rostrum and dolphin
chronicle.body: By its commander's order, Roman Navy marches from now on under the Rostrum and dolphin: bronze ship's ram beneath a dolphin.

chronicle.title: Lucius Papirius Cursor and Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges Back Messana Funds
chronicle.body: In the Senate, Lucius Papirius Cursor supported authorizing up to 3,000 from the treasury for the Messana operation, arguing that Rome had to hold the strait. Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges also supported the measure, but urged the Senate to keep the treasury’s cost in view.

quote.line: The strait must be held; vote the funds.
quote.speaker: Lucius Papirius Cursor
quote.occasion: in the Senate, urging authorization for the Messana operation

chronicle.title: Senate Approves a Fleet to Defend Rome’s Interests
chronicle.body: The admiral of the Roman fleet Manius Curius Dentatus, Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, Lucius Papirius Cursor, Tiberius Coruncanius, and Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges spoke in favor of permitting a Roman fleet to defend Rome’s interests. The Senate approved the measure 76 to 0, with 24 abstaining; patrician houses, landed families, and the Fabrician, Curian, Fabian, and Coruncanian circles supported it, while plebeian new men abstained.

quote.line: Rome needs ships to guard her own.
quote.speaker: Manius Curius Dentatus
quote.occasion: in the Senate as the fleet measure came to a vote

chronicle.title: Quintus Ogulnius Gallus Begins Organizing Silver for Rome’s Allies
chronicle.body: Quintus Ogulnius Gallus began organizing the use of Roman silver to support Rome’s allies while in Latium on the Almo.

chronicle.title: Statius Mettius Accepts Rome’s Terms for Talks on Messana’s Defence
chronicle.body: Statius Mettius, leader of the Mamertines of Messana, accepted the Roman consul Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio’s terms for discussing Rome’s protection against Syracusan attack: measures affecting Messana’s defence and the strait were to be settled in consultation. He requested practical talks that would preserve Messana’s self-rule.

quote.line: We will meet, and Messana will govern itself.
quote.speaker: Statius Mettius
quote.occasion: to Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio, accepting Rome’s terms for talks

chronicle.title: Manius Curius Dentatus Opens Deliberation on the Anio Water Works
chronicle.body: Manius Curius Dentatus, admiral of the Roman fleet, opened a public deliberation on authorizing and funding the Anio water works.

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina Finds His Estates in Order
chronicle.body: The consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina went through the books of his estates and found them in order.

chronicle.title: Lucanian Tribal Levy Runs Short of Bread Beneath Mons Vultur
chronicle.body: Word came to court that the Lucanian tribal levy had eaten the bread it carried and was on short rations beneath Mons Vultur in Daunia, where nothing fed it.

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina writes to Hanno of Carthage
chronicle.body: "We are withing our right, Messena is our protectorate" -- We are withing our right, Messena is our protectorate

chronicle.title: Roman field army is renamed Legio I
chronicle.body: By its commander's order, Roman field army is to be called Legio I from now on.

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina accepts Statius Mettius's letter
chronicle.body: "Protection for Messana" -- We accept Messena's protectorate. We shall defend Messena whenever they call for us, in exchange we shall receive money and manpower as well as your participation in any war Rome is in

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina Orders Legio I Carried to Messana
chronicle.body: Gaius Genucius Clepsina, the Roman consul, ordered the Roman navy to carry Legio I from Rome to Messana. The legion numbered 7,100 men and could not reach the northeastern coast of the Sikeloi by land. The nearest ships available to Roman power were allied Greek hulls on the southwestern coast, 610 km away and able to carry 540 men; they had to be ordered nearer first.

chronicle.title: Clepsina Proposes a Roman Naval Force of 150
chronicle.body: The Roman consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina proposed raising and equipping a naval force of 150. In the Senate, patrician houses, plebeian new men, and landed families backed his limited proposal. Clepsina fell gravely ill, and his household summoned care.

chronicle.title: The Senate Votes to Raise and Equip a Roman Naval Force
chronicle.body: The Senate voted to raise and equip a Roman naval force of 150. In eastern lowland Iazygia, a severe grain shortage had left people short of food and damaged local productive capacity; the magistrates could no longer conceal the shortfall.

chronicle.title: Yesbokheamani Becomes Head of the House After His Kinsman’s Death
chronicle.body: Prince Yesbokheamani of Kush lost a close senior kinsman, whose death left him head of the house and burdened with the family’s affairs.

quote.line: I bear the house now.
quote.speaker: Yesbokheamani
quote.occasion: as he took up the family’s affairs after his kinsman’s death

chronicle.title: Numidian Raiders Seize the Harvest in Inner Gaetulia
chronicle.body: Raiders from the Numidian kingdoms crossed into the inner uplands of north-western Gaetulia, seized the season’s harvest, and emptied villages. The Gaetuli faced a choice: whether to treat the raid as Numidian action or as brigandage.

chronicle.title: The Senate Votes to Raise and Equip a Roman Naval Force
chronicle.body: In the consulship of Gaius Genucius Clepsina, the Senate voted to raise and equip a Roman naval force of 150, carrying the measure 49 to 32, with 19 abstaining. The patrician houses supported it, the plebeian new men opposed it, and the landed families abstained.

chronicle.title: Romans Begin Raising and Equipping a Naval Force of 150
chronicle.body: The Romans began raising and equipping the naval force of 150.

chronicle.title: Manius Curius Dentatus Offers Rhegium Terms for Peace
chronicle.body: Manius Curius Dentatus sent Decius Vibellius, leader of the Campanian garrison at Rhegium, Rome’s terms for peace. They required the garrison to surrender the city and its arms and hand over those responsible for killing its citizens for Roman judgment.

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina writes to Decius Vibellius
chronicle.body: "Surrender and the only punishmenet you shall face is you and your men 10 years…" -- Surrender and the only punishmenet you shall face is you and your men 10 years in a punitive legion for rome under my command. After these 10 years you shall become citizens again

chronicle.title: Mamertines Appeal to Carthage for Messana’s Protection
chronicle.body: The Mamertines appealed to Carthage for protection of Messana, offering to consult with the Carthaginians over the city’s defence and interests rather than submit to Syracusan rule.

chronicle.title: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus Calls Gaius Genucius Clepsina a Traitor
chronicle.body: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus had promised Gaius Genucius Clepsina, the Roman consul, that he would not call him a traitor without proof. On the Almo in Latium, Fabricius broke that promise and called Clepsina a traitor without proof.

changes.label: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus
changes.detail: broke a promise to Gaius Genucius Clepsina: i will not call you a traitor without proof.

quote.line: You are a traitor.
quote.speaker: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus
quote.occasion: to Gaius Genucius Clepsina on the Almo, as he broke his promise

chronicle.title: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio Accepts Terms for the Rhegian Garrison
chronicle.body: The Roman consul Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio agreed to the terms set out in a letter from Decius Vibellius, leader of the Campanians at Rhegium: the garrison would serve ten years in Roman forces under Roman command, on assigned duties with ordinary provision, and Rome would take possession of Rhegium under the accepted peace terms. Blasio sent those terms to the garrison’s commander. “Ten years under Roman command; Rhegium passes to Rome,” he said as the terms were settled. Meanwhile, Statius Mettius, leader of the Mamertines, renewed his request to Rome for protection against Syracuse and asked to discuss terms promptly while preserving Messana’s self-rule.

quote.line: Ten years under Roman command; Rhegium passes to Rome.
quote.speaker: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio
quote.occasion: as he settled the garrison’s terms with Decius Vibellius

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina Reviews His Household Books
chronicle.body: The Roman consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina reviewed the household books he had opened to see whether any discrepancy appeared.

chronicle.title: Lucius Atilius Wins Goodwill with Public Games
chronicle.body: Lucius Atilius paid for costly public games in south-eastern Samnium, earning local goodwill and modest standing.

changes.label: Lucius Atilius
changes.detail: enters the record under Roman Republic

chronicle.title: Kaisaros of the Vaccaei Pays for a Costly Spectacle
chronicle.body: Kaisaros of the Vaccaei paid for a costly spectacle attended across the Uplands of the Mourbogoi. It won him substantial public standing and strengthened local cohesion.

chronicle.title: Manius Curius Dentatus Calls for an Inquiry into Clepsina’s Accounts
chronicle.body: In the Senate, Manius Curius Dentatus urged that the accusation that Clepsina had diverted public money be examined before judgment. The consul Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio opposed the inquiry, warning that it could turn rumor into a verdict.

quote.line: Let the accounts be examined before this matter is judged.
quote.speaker: Manius Curius Dentatus
quote.occasion: in the Senate, as he urged an inquiry into the accusation against Clepsina

chronicle.title: Western Albanian Buyers Drive Silver Prices Sharply Higher
chronicle.body: A rush of buyers for silver in the western uplands of Albania drove its price sharply higher as merchants competed for metal to pay troops and settle debts.

chronicle.title: Bennabels Faces Pressure to Save His Kinsman’s Lands
chronicle.body: A kinsman of Bennabels, the first chief of the Contestani, fell into debt, and a creditor’s demand publicly disgraced him. Bennabels faced pressure to intervene before the family lands were seized.

chronicle.title: Decius Vibellius Accepts Rome’s Peace Terms at Rhegium
chronicle.body: Decius Vibellius, leader of the Campanians at Rhegium, accepted Rome’s peace terms, yielding the city and its arms and agreeing to deliver those responsible for the killings for Roman judgment.

quote.line: Rhegium is yielded; let Rome judge the men it names.
quote.speaker: Decius Vibellius
quote.occasion: as he accepted Rome’s terms at Rhegium

chronicle.title: Manius Curius Dentatus Begins Survey for Bringing Anio Water to Rome
chronicle.body: Manius Curius Dentatus paid from his own purse to begin surveying a proposed route for bringing Anio water to Rome. The survey began in Latium, on the Almo.

chronicle.title: Fire Destroys Records in the South-eastern Samnite Hills
chronicle.body: Fire struck the heart of the Samnites’ south-eastern hills and took the records kept there.

chronicle.title: Senators Debate Raising Legio I for the Rhegium War
chronicle.body: In the Senate, the senator Lucius Postumius Megellus urged that Legio I be raised to 10,000 men, arguing that Rome had to show strength to its allies. The senator Tiberius Coruncanius opposed the increase, citing the accepted terms of surrender and the burden of enlarging the levy. The senator Gaius Fabricius Luscinus also opposed it, arguing that Rome should keep faith with the settlement rather than enlarge its army.

quote.line: Let Rhegium see Rome’s strength before doubt spreads among our allies.
quote.speaker: Lucius Postumius Megellus
quote.occasion: in the Senate, urging the increase

chronicle.title: Senators Debate Raising Legio I for Rhegium
chronicle.body: In the Senate, the senator Gaius Claudius Canina argued that Rhegium had yielded and Rome should make its protection certain. The senator Publius Valerius Laevinus urged the Senate to accept the surrender, judge the killers, and avoid an unnecessary levy; the senator Quintus Ogulnius Gallus argued that silver spent among Rome’s allies might secure more than another thousand spears. The senator Spurius Carvilius Maximus supported raising the legion to its full strength so Rome would be ready to keep Rhegium safe.

quote.line: Let the levy be full; Rome must be ready to keep Rhegium safe.
quote.speaker: Spurius Carvilius Maximus
quote.occasion: in the Senate, arguing for the levy

chronicle.title: The Senate Rejects a Larger Legion for the Rhegium War
chronicle.body: The Senate rejected a proposal to raise the First Legion to ten thousand men for the war at Rhegium. Fifty-one senators opposed it, and forty-nine abstained; none supported it. The consul Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio, Lucius Papirius Cursor, Lucius Postumius Megellus, and Spurius Carvilius Maximus spoke for the proposal. Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges, Manius Curius Dentatus, Tiberius Coruncanius, Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, Gaius Claudius Canina, Publius Valerius Laevinus, and Quintus Ogulnius Gallus spoke against it.

quote.line: Ten thousand? Rhegium will not have them.
quote.speaker: Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges
quote.occasion: in the Senate, as the proposal came to a vote

chronicle.title: Clepsina Sends Publius Nerius to Syracuse
chronicle.body: The Roman treasury sharply reduced the monthly wage paid to the Rhegian Punitive Legion. The consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina discreetly sent Publius Nerius to Syracuse to inquire into Syracusan intentions.

changes.label: Publius Nerius
changes.detail: enters the record under Roman Republic

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina Seeks a Larger Legion for the Rhegium War
chronicle.body: Gaius Genucius Clepsina, the Roman consul, put before the Senate a proposal to raise Legio I to ten thousand men for the war at Rhegium. He began seeking support for the levy: the plebeian new men backed it, while the patrician houses and landed families remained undecided. His fellow consul, Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio, favored a stronger field force. Clepsina warned the Roman people and the Republic’s allies that the war at Rhegium could spread if Rome failed to secure the strait and settle the garrison’s surrender. In Rome, a charge was laid that Clepsina had diverted public money to his household estates. In the Uplands of the Nicives, Zelalsan, prince of the Numidian kingdoms, had a mounted levy represented for the confederation’s own defense. In Central Gerrha, Abd al-Malik of Gerrha, the Gerrhaean ruler, organized a modest coast guard to protect the settlements and trade.

changes.label: Numidian Confederation Levy
changes.detail: raised under Numidian kingdoms at Uplands of the Nicives, 1k men

changes.label: Gerrhaean Coast Guard
changes.detail: raised under Gerrha (the Gerrhaeans) at Coast of the Thilouanoi, 500 men

changes.label: Abd al-Malik of Gerrha
changes.detail: enters the record under Gerrha (the Gerrhaeans)

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina accepts Statius Mettius's letter
chronicle.body: "Protection for Messana’s self-rule" -- Very well we shall send Legio I to defend you

chronicle.title: Lucius Papirius Cursor Spoke for Funding the Anio Water Works
chronicle.body: In the Senate, Lucius Papirius Cursor argued for public authorization and funding for the Anio water works.

quote.line: The war will end; Rome will still need water.
quote.speaker: Lucius Papirius Cursor
quote.occasion: in the Senate, as he argued for the water works

chronicle.title: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus Supports Funding for the Anio Water Works
chronicle.body: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus publicly supported authorization and funding for the Anio water works. In the Senate, Spurius Carvilius Maximus argued for the works, saying that Rome would still need water when the war ended.

quote.line: The war will end; Rome will still need water.
quote.speaker: Spurius Carvilius Maximus
quote.occasion: in the Senate, arguing for the Anio water works

chronicle.title: Lucius Postumius Megellus Opposes Funding for the Anio Water Works
chronicle.body: Tiberius Coruncanius publicly supported authorization and funding for the Anio water works. In the Senate, Lucius Postumius Megellus opposed them, arguing that wartime funds should go to immediate military needs.

quote.line: Keep the silver for the war; water can wait.
quote.speaker: Lucius Postumius Megellus
quote.occasion: in the Senate, opposing authorization and funding for the Anio water works

chronicle.title: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio Urges the Senate to Raise Legio I
chronicle.body: The Roman consul Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio spoke in the Senate for raising Legio I to 10,000 men for the war at Rhegium. He argued that a larger army would make Rhegium’s recovery more certain.

quote.line: A larger army will make recovery of Rhegium more certain.
quote.speaker: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio
quote.occasion: to the Senate, as he argued for raising Legio I

chronicle.title: Rome Sends Syracuse an Ultimatum over Messana
chronicle.body: Rome sent Syracuse an ultimatum demanding an end to hostilities against Messana and warning that continued attacks would bring open war.

chronicle.title: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio Accepts Messana’s Appeal for Roman Protection
chronicle.body: The consul Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio accepted Messana’s request for Roman protection against a Syracusan attack. He invited the city to discuss terms promptly, on condition that its self-rule be preserved.

quote.line: Rome will protect you; keep your own laws.
quote.speaker: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio
quote.occasion: to the Messanans, as he accepted their appeal

chronicle.title: Roman Navy Carries the Rhegian Punitive Legion to the Sikeloi Coast
chronicle.body: The Roman navy carried the Rhegian Punitive Legion across in a single crossing, and it arrived on the north-eastern coast of the Sikeloi.

chronicle.title: Manius Curius Dentatus Urges the Senate to Aid Rome’s Allies
chronicle.body: The admiral Manius Curius Dentatus urged the Senate to use Roman silver to support Rome’s allies, arguing that Rome must not leave them unaided. Quintus Ogulnius Gallus urged that the silver reach the allies before their faith in Rome was spent. Gaius Fabricius Luscinus argued that Rome must stand with the allies if it expected them to stand with Rome.

quote.line: If we ask our allies to stand with Rome, Rome must stand with them.
quote.speaker: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus
quote.occasion: speaking on "Use Roman silver to support Rome's allies"

chronicle.title: Lucius Papirius Cursor Urges a Larger Legion for the Rhegium War
chronicle.body: The senator Lucius Papirius Cursor urged the Senate to raise Legio I to 10,000 for the Rhegium war, arguing that Rome must arrive in strength. The senator Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges opposed the increase, saying the peace terms had been accepted and expansion would be costly. The senator Manius Curius Dentatus also argued against it, favouring an orderly settlement after the garrison accepted surrender terms.

quote.line: Rhegium must see Rome arrive in strength.
quote.speaker: Lucius Papirius Cursor
quote.occasion: in the Senate, urging the increase

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina Warns Hieron II Over Messana
chronicle.body: The Roman consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina wrote to Hieron II, king of Syracuse, demanding that he cease hostilities against Messana. Clepsina warned that continued attacks would be treated as an invitation to war. Rome had undertaken to protect Messana while preserving the city’s self-rule and right to be heard. He then ordered Legio I to Messana by the Roman fleet. The legion numbered some seven thousand men, but the nearest allied Greek ships lay on the Sikeloi’s southwest coast, about six hundred kilometres away, and could carry only about five hundred and forty. The ships had first to be ordered nearer.

quote.line: Cease hostilities against Messana.
quote.speaker: Gaius Genucius Clepsina
quote.occasion: in his letter to Hieron II

chronicle.title: Manius Curius Dentatus Begins the Anio Water Works
chronicle.body: After the Senate authorized and funded the Anio water works, the admiral Manius Curius Dentatus began construction.

quote.line: Bring the water to Rome.
quote.speaker: Manius Curius Dentatus
quote.occasion: as work began on the Anio water works

chronicle.title: The Senate Authorizes Treasury Funds for the Messana Operation
chronicle.body: The Senate authorized up to 3,000 from the treasury for the Messana operation; seventy-two voted for the measure and twenty-eight abstained. The patrician houses and the circles of Fabricius, Curius, Fabius, Coruncanius, and Claudius supported it, while the plebeian newcomers and landed families abstained. Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, Lucius Papirius Cursor, and Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges spoke in its favor.

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina Moves to Investigate Manius Curius Dentatus
chronicle.body: The consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina moved that the Senate investigate Manius Curius Dentatus’s conduct in bringing the accusation. The Senate left the motion pending.

chronicle.title: Tiberius Coruncanius Reports No Divine Sign Showing Carthage Hostile
chronicle.body: Tiberius Coruncanius reported to the consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina that he knew of no divine sign warranting the treatment of Carthage as a threat. He urged Rome to take the signs as a warning to act prudently, not as proof of Carthaginian hostility.

quote.line: I accept the ten years; my men will live.
quote.speaker: Decius Vibellius
quote.occasion: Accepting Rome’s surrender terms

chronicle.title: Roman Senators Urge Examination of the Charge Against Clepsina
chronicle.body: In the Senate, Lucius Papirius Cursor urged that the accusation that Clepsina had diverted public money be examined. “Let the accounts be opened; let the evidence speak.” Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges also called for an examination, but said judgment should wait for proof. Tiberius Coruncanius and Gaius Fabricius Luscinus likewise urged that the charge be tested and the evidence heard before judgment.

quote.line: Let the accounts be opened; let the evidence speak.
quote.speaker: Lucius Papirius Cursor
quote.occasion: in the Senate, as he urged examination of the accusation against Clepsina

chronicle.title: Manius Curius Dentatus Urges the Senate to Examine His Conduct
chronicle.body: Manius Curius Dentatus spoke in the Senate in favor of examining his conduct in bringing the charge against Clepsina. He asked the senators to examine his conduct as fully as the charge.

quote.line: Let the Senate examine my conduct as fully as the charge.
quote.speaker: Manius Curius Dentatus
quote.occasion: to the Senate, as it considered examining his conduct

chronicle.title: Carthaginian Fleet Enters Mamertine Land on the Northeastern Sikeloi Coast
chronicle.body: The Carthaginian fleet reached the northeastern coast of the Sikeloi and entered land belonging to the Mamertines of Messana without their leave.

chronicle.title: Gaius Claudius Canina and Publius Valerius Laevinus Urge an Examination of Clepsina’s Accusation
chronicle.body: In the Senate, the senator Gaius Claudius Canina urged that the accusation that Clepsina had diverted public money be examined and the accounts opened. The senator Publius Valerius Laevinus also called for an examination, arguing that the charge should be judged by its evidence rather than by the quarrel.

quote.line: Let the accounts be opened; Rome is served by a clean reckoning.
quote.speaker: Gaius Claudius Canina
quote.occasion: in the Senate, urging examination of the accusation against Clepsina

chronicle.title: Three Senators Urge Inquiry into Dentatus’s Charge Against Clepsina
chronicle.body: In the Senate, the senator Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges urged an inquiry into Manius Curius Dentatus’s conduct in bringing the charge against Clepsina, arguing that Rome should protect its allies by judging fairly. The senator Tiberius Coruncanius likewise urged the Senate to examine both the conduct and the charge, and to let proof guide its judgment. The senator Gaius Fabricius Luscinus urged the Senate to hear the evidence of Dentatus’s conduct and judge only what it proved.

quote.line: Hear the evidence of his conduct, and judge only what it proves.
quote.speaker: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus
quote.occasion: speaking on "Investigate Manius Curius Dentatus's conduct in bringing the charge against Clepsina"

chronicle.title: Rome Crosses to Messana and Goes to War with Carthage
chronicle.body: The Roman consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina ordered Legio I from Latium to Messana, but the legion remained in Latium while the navy was already at Messana. Rome’s Punitive Legion and navy crossed to Messana; Carthage opposed Rome’s presence at the strait, and the two powers went to war. A private creditor called in a debt beyond what Clepsina could raise that season.

chronicle.title: Gaius Genucius Clepsina Denies Diverting Public Money and Seeks a Fleet
chronicle.body: The consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina publicly denied diverting public money, calling the charge false, and called for scrutiny of corruption and misuse of power, including his accuser’s conduct. He opened a Senate debate on providing Rome with a fleet to defend its interests, continuing the existing naval project. Clepsina ordered a delegation to ask Tiberius Coruncanius, a pontiff, whether the gods were warning Rome about Carthage; the delegation put the question to him.

quote.line: Ask the Pontifex whether the gods are warning Rome about Carthage.
quote.speaker: Gaius Genucius Clepsina
quote.occasion: to the delegation, as he ordered it to put the question to Tiberius Coruncanius

chronicle.title: Carvilius, Papirius, and Canina Back Aid for Rome's Allies
chronicle.body: In the Senate, the senator Spurius Carvilius Maximus and the senator Lucius Papirius Cursor publicly supported using Roman silver to aid Rome's allies. The senator Gaius Claudius Canina also spoke for the proposal.

quote.line: Allied arms must not go unpaid.
quote.speaker: Gaius Claudius Canina
quote.occasion: in the Senate debate on aid to Rome's allies

chronicle.title: A Faction Forms Around Gaius Claudius Canina
chronicle.body: A faction formed in the Roman Republic around Gaius Claudius Canina.

chronicle.title: Rome Takes Rhegium Under the Peace Terms
chronicle.body: Rhegium was surrendered under the accepted peace terms and passed to Roman control without a storming or sack. Rome organized the Campanian garrison as the Rhegian Punitive Legion under the agreed terms of punitive service; with the city, Rome gained the south-western coast of the Sikeloi. The consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina continued to deny diverting public funds and said the evidence would establish his innocence. He opened his household books for an auditor to inspect. The consul Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio’s household began arranging a marriage alliance for a close family member, bringing a modest obligation to his attention. A marriage proposal from a neighboring Sequani household reached Britomaros, ruler of the Sequani, and called for him to consider an alliance between their families.

changes.label: South-western coast of the Sikeloi
changes.detail: passes from Bruttians to Roman Republic

changes.label: Rhegian Punitive Legion
changes.detail: raised under Roman Republic at South-western coast of the Sikeloi, 1k men

quote.line: Open the books; the evidence will clear me.
quote.speaker: Gaius Genucius Clepsina
quote.occasion: as he opened his household books for the auditor

chronicle.title: Manius Curius Dentatus Pays for Games in the Volscian Hills
chronicle.body: In the Hills of the Volsci, Manius Curius Dentatus paid for costly public games. They won him popular acclaim and left the province in better spirits.

chronicle.title: Senate Orders Examination of Clepsina’s Alleged Diversion of Public Money
chronicle.body: Manius Curius Dentatus, Lucius Papirius Cursor, Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges, Tiberius Coruncanius, Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, and Gaius Claudius Canina spoke for examining the accusation that Clepsina had diverted public money. Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio, the consul, spoke against it, but the Senate carried the motion by 100 votes to none.

quote.line: Examine the accusation that Clepsina diverted public money.
quote.speaker: Manius Curius Dentatus
quote.occasion: in the Senate, speaking for an examination

chronicle.title: The Senate Approves Roman Silver for Rome’s Allies
chronicle.body: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio, the Roman consul, publicly supported using Roman silver to aid Rome’s allies before the Senate vote. The Senate carried the proposal 100 to 0, with the patrician houses, plebeian new men, landed families, and the Fabrician, Curian, Fabian, Coruncanian, and Claudian circles in favour.

chronicle.title: A Storm Takes the Season’s Grain Convoy on the Clanius
chronicle.body: A storm off southeastern Campania on the Clanius took the season’s grain convoy.

chronicle.title: The Senate Orders an Inquiry into Manius Curius Dentatus's Charge Against Clepsina
chronicle.body: The Senate voted 100 to 0 to investigate Manius Curius Dentatus's conduct in bringing the charge against the Roman consul Gaius Genucius Clepsina. Dentatus, Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges, Tiberius Coruncanius, and Gaius Fabricius Luscinus spoke in favour of the inquiry.

chronicle.title: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio Makes Roman Protection of Messana Conditional on Consultation
chronicle.body: After Statius Mettius, leader of the Mamertines of Messana, sought terms for Roman protection, the Roman consul Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio replied that Rome would discuss the matter promptly. He said Messana must consult Rome on measures affecting its defence and the strait; Rome would hear the Mamertines’ claim to self-rule and seek to deter a Syracusan attack.

quote.line: No protection without counsel over the strait.
quote.speaker: Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio
quote.occasion: to Statius Mettius, as he answered Messana’s request for terms

chronicle.title: Hieron II Arranges Consultation with Carthage
chronicle.body: Hieron II, king of Syracuse, heard the Mamertines’ terms and settled a procedure for consulting Carthage before further action at the strait. He sought to contain the Mamertines through talks and secure Syracuse, while keeping secret the possibility that Rome might intervene if the crisis worsened; he also began handing part of the government to others, judging the burden too great for one man.

chronicle.title: Hieron II Rejects Rome’s Demand, and Rome Makes War on Syracuse
chronicle.body: The Roman Republic sent Hieron II, king of Syracuse, a letter demanding that Syracuse cease hostilities against Messana. Hieron refused, saying Syracuse would maintain its present pause and hear Messana’s terms, but that he could not accept Rome’s demand as a renunciation of Syracuse’s claim or its right to negotiate. The Roman Republic then made war on the Kingdom of Syracuse, as the letter had warned it would.

quote.line: I cannot accept Rome’s demand as a renunciation of our claim or of our right to negotiate.
quote.speaker: Hieron II
quote.occasion: in his refusal of Rome’s demand

chronicle.title: Survivors and Chiefs Give Separate Accounts of the Gaetulian Raiders
chronicle.body: The survivors and chiefs gave separate written particulars of the raiders’ marks and their route of retreat.

chronicle.title: Roman Navy Completes Its Fleet of 150 Warships
chronicle.body: The Roman Navy completed its fleet of 150 warships and stood ready.

chronicle.title: Manius Curius Dentatus, Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, and Lucius Papirius Cursor Debate a Roman Fleet
chronicle.body: In the Senate, the Roman senator Manius Curius Dentatus argued that a fleet would keep faith with allies who trusted Rome’s protection. Gaius Fabricius Luscinus urged that ships guard the allies and that proof, rather than accusation, judge a man. Lucius Papirius Cursor argued that a fleet would give Rome reach wherever the allies needed its strength.

quote.line: A fleet keeps faith with the allies who trust our protection.
quote.speaker: Manius Curius Dentatus
quote.occasion: in the Senate, supporting a Roman fleet

chronicle.title: Clepsina Transfers 200 from the Roman Treasury to the Allied Greek Fleet
chronicle.body: Clepsina transferred 200 from the Roman treasury to the war chest of the Allied Greek hulls to support the fleet.

chronicle.title: Apulian Cities and Other Peoples Send Men to Rome’s War with Carthage
chronicle.body: The Apulian cities, Bruttians, Etruscan cities, Lucanians, Marsi and Paeligni, Picentes, Samnites, and Umbrians sent about twenty-six thousand men to the Roman Republic’s war with Carthage, as their treaty bound them.

storylines.title: Rhegium and the Campanian Legion
storylines.stakes: Rome’s treatment of Rhegium and its garrison will be watched by its Italian allies.
history: The Campanian legion sent to hold Rhegium killed its citizens and took the city for itself.
The Senate has resolved that the matter be ended.
Manius Curius Dentatus sent Rome's peace terms to the Campanian garrison, demanding Rhegium and the men responsible for the killings.
Decius accepted Rome’s peace terms, yielding Rhegium and its arms and agreeing to deliver those responsible for the killings for Roman judgment.

Rome's peace terms have been accepted: Rhegium and its arms are yielded, and those responsible for the killings are to be delivered for Roman judgment. Possession and judgment remain to be carried out.
Decius accepted Rome’s peace terms, yielding Rhegium and its arms and agreeing to deliver those responsible for the killings for Roman judgment.
Decius answered Clepsina’s letter by accepting the ten-year punitive service terms and the surrender of Rhegium and its arms.
Rome has taken possession of Rhegium under the accepted surrender. The surrendered men are organized as a punitive service force pending the judgment and administration of their terms.
Manius Curius Dentatus opened a Senate deliberation on the judgment and administration of the delivered men's ten-year punitive service.
Curius placed the practical administration of the Campanian Legion's punitive service before the Senate for determination.
storylines.nextDevelopment: The Senate determines and records the service terms.

storylines.title: The Messana Crisis
storylines.stakes: Messana's safety and self-rule remain threatened; Syracuse's claim and Carthage's unresolved position keep the crisis open.
history: Hieron accepted Carthage's detailed consultation timetable, committing Syracuse to notice and a meeting before relevant action while leaving its claim against Messana unresolved.
Mettius pressed Rome for a concrete account of protection as Syracuse's threat to Messana continued.
Mettius secured a further month of provisions for the Mamertine garrison as he continued to hold Messana against the Syracusan threat.
Mettius sent Hieron a written proposal: Syracuse should give notice and consult the Mamertines and Carthage before any action affecting Messana or the strait.

Hieron received Mettius and heard his consultation proposal; Syracuse has already accepted advance notice and consultation with Carthage, but no decision on Messana's government or Syracuse's claim was made.
Mettius met Hieron and presented the Mamertine case for advance notice and consultation before Syracusan action affecting Messana or the strait.
Hanno accepted Syracuse’s concrete notice and consultation terms, but again declined the Mamertines’ request for Carthaginian military protection.
Hanno reaffirmed Carthage’s agreed notice and consultation procedure to Hieron, stressing that it requires consultation but does not commit Carthage to intervene.
Hieron reaffirmed that Syracuse would observe the agreed advance-notice and consultation procedure before further action affecting the strait.
Hieron answered Rome by maintaining Syracuse’s pause while rejecting Rome’s demand as a limit on his claim, and asked Carthage to hold the agreed consultation promptly.
Hanno answered Mettius by withholding a promise of armed protection while offering immediate consultation, and wrote Hieron proposing written notice terms as the Syracusan pause continues.
Hanno invited Mettius to set out guarantees for Messana that would not require Carthaginian armed intervention.
Mettius answered Hanno’s invitation with proposals for guarantees that preserve Messana’s self-rule without requiring Carthaginian armed intervention.
Hieron accepted Carthage’s prompt consultation and sent Mettius a written proposal for a pause while Messana’s security and self-rule are discussed.
Mettius sent Hieron a renewed written request for guarantees preserving Messana’s self-rule during a pause in Syracusan advances, while keeping the garrison ready.

Hieron sent Mettius written temporary guarantees: Syracuse will maintain a pause in advances on Messana while talks proceed, and Messana’s self-rule and right to be heard remain in place during the pause; Syracuse’s claim is reserved.
Mettius renewed his written demand for practical guarantees that preserve Messana’s self-rule during the pause, and asked Hieron to state the terms plainly while the garrison remains ready.
Mettius sent Hieron concrete terms for a written pause, preserving Messana's self-rule as an open question and requiring consultation before further action.

Hieron accepted Mettius's request for talks on a pause and sent written interim guarantees: no advance during negotiations, self-rule open to agreement, Syracuse's claim reserved, and consultation with Carthage before further action.
Hieron confirmed the interim guarantees to Mettius and accepted Carthage's immediate consultation, keeping the pause in force while practical terms are discussed.
Mettius accepted Hieron's written interim guarantees as a basis for talks, while insisting that Messana's self-rule is not surrendered and seeking practical safeguards.
Hanno renewed Carthage's request for prompt consultation with Syracuse on Messana and the strait, asking that notice terms be recorded before either side acts.
Hieron sent Mettius a written proposal to meet promptly and settle practical safeguards for the agreed pause, while preserving Messana's self-rule and Syracuse's claim.

Hieron sent Mettius a written draft of practical safeguards: the pause continues, Messana governs itself during talks, and Syracuse will not act against it before completing consultation with Carthage.
storylines.nextDevelopment: Mettius answers the draft and the parties settle the written terms of the pause.

storylines.title: Hieron II and Gaius Genucius Clepsina
storylines.stakes: Carthaginian consultation may constrain the timing of Syracuse’s action at Messana without settling its claim to the city.
history: Hieron sent Carthage a request to settle prompt notice and consultation before any action at Messana affecting the strait, while reserving Syracuse’s claim against the city.
Hieron proposed immediate notice and a consultation meeting within five days before action affecting the strait or Carthaginian western possessions.
storylines.nextDevelopment: Carthage answers Syracuse’s proposed notice procedure.

storylines.title: The Gaetulian Frontier Raid
storylines.stakes: A devastated harvest and emptied villages press Gaetuli to determine whether the raid was brigandage or an act of the Numidian kingdoms.
history: Iepmatath referred the question of responsibility for the frontier raid to his confederation's council, opening a deliberation on whether to seek redress from Numidia or treat the raiders as unaffiliated.
Iepmatath pressed the chiefs to bring their deliberation on responsibility for the frontier raid to a decision on whether Gaetuli should seek redress.
Iepmatath put the question of seeking redress for the frontier raid to a vote of the chiefs.
The chiefs approved seeking redress for the frontier raid by 26 votes to none, with 12 abstentions; the war-bands supported the motion while several regional chiefs abstained.
Iepmatath began an inquiry into whether a Numidian kingdom directed the frontier raid or whether the raiders acted independently.
Iepmatath sent inquiries to frontier survivors and local chiefs, seeking accounts of the raiders’ identity and retreat.
Hanno renewed his request to Hieron for advance notice and a prompt consultation before action affecting Messana, the strait, or Carthaginian western possessions.
Iepmatath renewed the inquiry, dispatching requests for testimony from frontier survivors and local chiefs about the raiders' identity and retreat.
Iepmatath renewed requests for testimony from frontier survivors and local chiefs, continuing the inquiry into the raiders’ identity and retreat.
Iepmatath ordered the returned testimony and the renewed inquiries gathered for comparison before deciding whether to address a Numidian kingdom.
Iepmatath renewed the summons for survivors and local chiefs to give testimony identifying the raiders and their retreat, then ordered the accounts compared.
Iepmatath convened the gathered frontier survivors and local chiefs to compare their accounts for consistent descriptions, identifying marks, and a route of retreat.

Iepmatath ordered the gathered chiefs and survivors to provide separate written accounts of identifying marks and the raiders' retreat, so those details can be checked against the testimony already compared.
Iepmatath compared the gathered written particulars against the testimony already collected, checking the raiders’ identifying marks and retreat route for corroboration.

Iepmatath judged that the corroborated particulars do not identify a Numidian kingdom with sufficient certainty to hold one responsible; he treated the raiders as unaffiliated pending clearer evidence.
storylines.nextDevelopment: Seek any further evidence that could connect the raiders to a Numidian kingdom, or close the inquiry as brigandage.

storylines.title: The health of Menecrates
storylines.stakes: Whether Menecrates lives out the year, and what falls apart if he does not.
history: Menecrates has been unwell since the turn of the season.
Menecrates hired Damon, a physician, for a term of ninety days to attend his continuing illness.
During his confinement, Menecrates continued the physician's attendance for the illness that had not passed; no change in his health was established.
storylines.nextDevelopment: Whether the physician's continuing treatment improves Menecrates's health.

storylines.title: The Charge Against Clepsina
storylines.stakes: Rome’s treatment of Rhegium and its garrison will be watched by its Italian allies.
history: Curius opened a Senate deliberation on practical terms for the Campanian Legion’s punitive service, carrying forward the Senate’s judgment of the delivered men.
Curius placed the practical administration of the Campanian Legion's punitive service before the Senate for determination.
storylines.nextDevelopment: The Senate determines and records the service terms.

storylines.title: The health of Trebius Ninnius
storylines.stakes: Whether Trebius Ninnius lives out the year, and what falls apart if he does not.
history: Trebius Ninnius has been unwell since the turn of the season.
Trebius summoned local healers to attend his continuing sickness.
Trebius submitted to a further examination by the local healers he had summoned, seeking relief from the sickness that has persisted.
storylines.nextDevelopment: Whether the healers can ease Trebius's sickness, and whether he will entrust any burdens of rule to others.

storylines.title: The health of Dubnocoveros
storylines.stakes: Whether Dubnocoveros lives out the year, and what falls apart if he does not.
history: Dubnocoveros has been unwell since the turn of the season.
Dubnocoveros commissioned a physician to attend his lingering illness.
Dubnocoveros hired a physician for a ninety-day term to attend his lingering illness.
Dubnocoveros withdrew from public duties and took to bed while his lingering illness was attended.
Dubnocoveros continued resting in bed while the physician attended his lingering illness; no improvement or decline was established.
storylines.nextDevelopment: Whether rest and the physician's continued attendance improve Dubnocoveros's health.

storylines.title: A hidden Genucian inquiry
storylines.stakes: Whether the accusation of diverting public funds is substantiated, and whether Clepsina can retain the confidence of the Senate.
history: Gaius Genucius quietly continued his inquiry, sounding out household retainers for gossip that might unsettle Clepsina's standing.
Gaius discreetly questioned household retainers about Clepsina's affairs, seeking gossip that might unsettle his standing.
The Senate-authorized inquiry is now assigned to Gaius Fabricius Luscinus for an independent evidence-based examination.
storylines.nextDevelopment: The examiner reviews the relevant public and household accounts and reports whether evidence substantiates the charge.

storylines.title: Something laid against Hieron II
storylines.stakes: Whether Hieron II lives out the year, and who is found to have wanted otherwise.
history: Gaius Genucius Clepsina set something in motion, and told nobody who did not need to know.
storylines.nextDevelopment: Whether the hand gets near enough, and whether anybody talks first.

storylines.title: Messana appeals to Carthage
storylines.stakes: Messana's safety and self-rule remain threatened; Syracuse's claim and Carthage's unresolved position keep the crisis open.
history: Mettius accepted Hieron’s meeting invitation and insisted that talks address Messana’s safety and self-rule.
Mettius accepted Hieron's invitation to meet within five days and renewed Messana's appeal to Carthage after Rome's silence.
Hieron answered Mettius’s renewed meeting request, accepting continued talks and the pause in advances while reserving Syracuse’s claim.

Hieron answers Hanno that Syracuse will give advance notice before any action affecting Messana, the strait, or Carthaginian western possessions, and asks Carthage to name an envoy for continued consultation while talks with Mettius proceed.
Hieron sent Mettius practical terms for continuing negotiations and reaffirmed Syracuse’s advance-notice procedure to Carthage.
Mettius sought a direct clarification from Rome about protection and Messana’s self-rule while Syracuse’s proposed terms remain under discussion.
Hieron sent Mettius a fresh invitation to state Messana’s terms, reaffirming the pause in advances and Syracuse’s reservation of its claim.
Mettius renewed his appeal to Carthage for protection that would deter Syracuse while preserving Messana’s self-rule.
Hanno answered Messana’s renewed appeals by offering discussion of practical guarantees but refusing a promise of Carthaginian protection or military intervention.
Mettius pressed Hanno for a definite answer on whether Carthage would deter a Syracusan attack, and asked for a practical alternative if it would not.
Hanno answered Mettius, declining a firm protection pledge but offering consultation with Syracuse and practical guarantees for Messana's self-rule.
Mettius accepted Rome's offer of protection against a Syracusan attack on the stated terms of preserving Messana's self-rule, and requested practical talks.
Mettius accepted Rome’s terms for discussing protection and consultation, and requested practical arrangements that preserve Messana’s self-rule.
Mettius accepted Rome’s terms for discussion, requested practical protection during negotiations, and renewed his demand to Syracuse for written guarantees during the pause.
Hieron accepted Hanno’s invitation to consultation and sent Mettius written terms proposing a pause while Messana’s security is discussed.
Mettius sent Hieron a renewed written request for guarantees preserving Messana’s self-rule during a pause and kept the garrison ready.
Hieron sent Mettius written temporary guarantees for a pause and preservation of Messana’s self-rule during talks, reserving Syracuse’s claim.
Mettius renewed his request to Hieron for written practical guarantees preserving Messana’s self-rule during the pause.
Mettius stated practical guarantees to Hieron while keeping the garrison ready; Carthage has refused to promise armed protection but remains available for consultation.
Hanno renewed Carthage's invitation to discuss practical guarantees while restating that Carthage would not promise armed intervention.
Hieron accepted Carthage's immediate consultation and confirmed the pause and written guarantees to Mettius.

Mettius answered Carthage's renewed invitation with practical proposals: written assurances for the Syracusan pause and self-rule, continued consultation, and a diplomatic response to any breach, without demanding armed intervention.
Hanno renewed Carthage's invitation for concrete proposals on guarantees for Messana that do not require Carthaginian armed intervention, and kept the consultation channel open.
Hieron sent Hanno written notice that he is proposing practical safeguards to Mettius and requested consultation before any further action affecting Messana or the strait.
storylines.nextDevelopment: Hanno answers the notice and the parties hold consultation on the safeguards.
